extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists and fiction writers interested in writing epistolary novels
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, writing, and structuring a novel told through letters, diary entries, and other documents, with emphasis on voice, format choice, pacing, and plot advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define your characters' voices early
rubrics_metrics.description: Give each character a distinct style. A romantic might use flowery language, while a skeptic keeps it short and to the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page recommends establishing distinct voices early so readers can identify speakers immediately. Examples: Daddy-Long-Legs (wonder and growth), Dear Committee Members (dry academic wit). Technique: tailor vocabulary and sentence structure to reflect background, education, and personality. Anti-pattern: characters who sound alike or whose voice shifts inconsistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make each letter/entry feel authentic
rubrics_metrics.description: Each letter or diary entry must feel genuine as if written by a real person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity involves matching register, tone, and the writer's relationship to the recipient. The article stresses that every 'letter' should serve a purpose and feel like private, unfiltered thought when appropriate. Anti-patterns include entries that read like author exposition or contrived summaries rather than believable documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure coherence despite fragmented storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must ensure coherence despite fragmented storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because epistolary novels present narrative in pieces, writers should help readers piece the story together through careful sequencing, consistent plotting, and purposeful document selection. Examples cited: use of letters to slowly unveil plot, avoid confusion by maintaining through-lines. Anti-pattern: a fragmented sequence that leaves readers unable to follow the main plot or character motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use each document to advance the plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Use letters to reveal key plot points: each entry should drive the story forward, offering insight into character motivations or uncovering secrets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The advice is to avoid filler—entries must add value to the narrative. Entries can reveal crucial information or hint at backstory. Technique: strategically place revelations and cliffhangers in documents to maintain momentum. Anti-pattern: long diary passages that reveal nothing new and stall the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance intimacy with plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters are personal, but they need to serve the story. Avoid entries that feel like filler, focusing instead on ones that add value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the emotional immediacy and intimacy the form provides while ensuring that those intimate moments connect to the larger narrative. The page frames this as balancing personal detail with narrative utility. Anti-patterns: over-personalized rambling that doesn't relate to plot or theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the right format for tone, pacing, and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Select from letters, diary entries, newspaper articles, emails, texts, etc., because the format will significantly impact tone, pacing, and overall structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letters between characters create intimacy and immediacy; diary entries are introspective; newspaper/public documents provide objectivity and context. Consider how each format influences reader perception and pick formats that match your story’s needs. Example guidance: use diary for private thoughts; use public documents to ground historical novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define the purpose of each document type
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider what each format will contribute to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly plan what each diary entry, letter, or clipping accomplishes (reveal emotion, advance plot, provide context). Technique: write in the appropriate perspective (e.g., first-person for diaries) and choose details that reveal character traits or emotional states. Anti-pattern: using multiple document types without clear distinct functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public documents sparingly and intentionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporating newspaper articles, reports, or official documents can ground your story, but use them sparingly to avoid interrupting the narrative flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public documents offer objectivity and broader context; they are effective for historical grounding or showing societal impact. The page advises a well-placed news clipping can add authenticity without overwhelming the main narrative. Anti-pattern: overuse of clippings that break immersion or slow pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix formats for a layered narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine letters, diary entries, and news articles to create a multi-dimensional view of the story’s world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article suggests starting with diary entries to introduce a protagonist, then gradually adding letters from others and sprinkling public documents to shift focus outward. Mixing formats deepens perspective and can build suspense or contrast private vs. public selves. Technique: plan sequencing so format shifts enhance rather than confuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage multiple points of view without an omniscient narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Present multiple points of view through documents to create a rich, multi-faceted narrative without relying on an omniscient narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each document type or correspondent allows a different perspective; ensure clarity by making voices distinct and signaling who is writing. The epistolary form's advantage is multiple viewpoints, but it requires careful management to avoid reader confusion. Anti-pattern: POVs that blur together or contradict in ways that aren’t purposeful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing and timing of letters/entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully consider the timing and spacing of the letters or diary entries to create tension, suspense, and proper narrative rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cliffhangers, withhold information, or pace revelations to keep readers engaged. The article highlights timing as crucial to maintaining momentum. Anti-patterns include uneven spacing or too many routine entries that sap forward motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor voice techniques to document type
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt techniques appropriate to the form: e.g., write diary entries in first person and use sentence fragments to mirror anxiety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/techniques given: first-person for diaries, short fragmented sentences to mirror a character’s anxious state, vocabulary choices that reflect education/background. These micro-level choices help make documents feel authentic and emotionally resonant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain internal consistency across voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure consistency of character voice and style across the novel without sacrificing authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While characters’ voices must be distinct, they must also remain consistent over time (unless an intentional development/change). The page mentions using editing tools to refine voices and keep them coherent across many entries. Anti-pattern: sudden unexplained shifts in diction, knowledge, or tone that break believability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the epistolary format to create suspense and strategic revelation
rubrics_metrics.description: Withhold information or reveal it through selected documents to create suspense and keep readers engaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can place key revelations in letters or entries to control what readers learn and when. The article highlights cliffhangers and gradual unveiling as effective tactics. Anti-pattern: revealing everything too early or never resolving hinted mysteries.
